insert.title: How HashMap::insert works
insert.description: Stores a value under a key; returns the old value if the key was already there.

slides.caption: A HashMap stores each key once. Inserting a key that exists replaces its value.
"a" is new: it is stored with 1, and insert returns None.
"a" exists already: 5 replaces 1, and the old 1 is returned.
Check the returned Option when you need to know whether something was overwritten.

get.title: How HashMap::get works
get.description: Looks a key up; returns Some(&value) or None.

slides.caption: get hashes the key and jumps straight to where its value would be. No searching through all entries.
"a" is in the map: Some(&1).
"z" is not: None, no panic.
m["a"] also works but panics for a missing key. get is the safe version.

get_mut.title: How HashMap::get_mut works
get_mut.description: Borrows a value mutably so you can change it in place.

slides.caption: get_mut gives a &mut to the value stored under the key.
"a" is found; v points at its value, 1.
*v += 10 changes the value inside the map to 11.
For "insert if missing, otherwise update", the entry API is shorter.

contains_key.title: How HashMap::contains_key works
contains_key.description: Checks whether a key is in the map.

slides.caption: contains_key only looks at keys, quickly, by hashing.
"b" hashes to a slot that holds "b": true.
The value (2) is not needed for the answer.
If you need the value afterwards, use get once instead of contains_key followed by get.

remove.title: How HashMap::remove works
remove.description: Removes a key and returns its value.

slides.caption: remove takes the entry out of the map and hands you the value.
"a" is found and taken out: Some(1).
The map is left with just "b". Removing a missing key returns None.
remove_entry returns the key too.

entry.title: How HashMap::entry works
entry.description: Gets the slot for a key, filled or empty, so you can insert or update in one lookup.

slides.caption: entry("a") finds the place where "a" lives (or would live). Then you decide what to do with it.
"a" exists, so entry gives an Occupied entry pointing at 1.
or_insert does not insert anything here and returns &mut 1; += 1 makes it 2.
With a missing key, entry would be Vacant and or_insert(0) would insert 0 first.

or_insert.title: How Entry::or_insert works
or_insert.description: Inserts a default if the key is missing, then lends you the value: word counting in one line.

slides.caption: For each word: if it has no count yet, insert 0; then add 1 to the count.
"a" is new: 0 is inserted, then 0 + 1 = 1.
"b" is new too: 1.
"a" is there already: or_insert keeps 1, and 1 + 1 = 2.
This is the classic Rust counting idiom. or_default() does the same for types with a default (0 for numbers).

or_insert_with.title: How Entry::or_insert_with works
or_insert_with.description: Like or_insert, but the default is built by a closure only when needed.

slides.caption: For each pair, find the team's list; create an empty Vec only the first time.
"red" is new: Vec::new runs, then "ann" is pushed.
"blue" is new: another empty Vec, then "bo".
"red" exists: the closure is not called; "cy" joins the existing list.
Grouping items by a key: one of the most useful things a HashMap does.

and_modify.title: How Entry::and_modify works
and_modify.description: Changes the value if the key exists; chain or_insert for when it does not.

slides.caption: and_modify runs only for an existing key. or_insert runs only for a missing one.
"a" exists: and_modify adds 1, making 2. or_insert does nothing.
"z" is missing: and_modify is skipped, and or_insert stores 1.
Reads naturally: "if there, add one; otherwise start at one".

or_default.title: How Entry::or_default works
or_default.description: Inserts the type's default value (0, "", empty Vec) if the key is missing.

slides.caption: or_default is or_insert with the default of the value type: 0 for counters.
h, e: each gets 0, then 1.
The first l: 0, then 1. The second l: already 1, so 2.
The value type must implement Default. Numbers, String, Vec and HashMap all do.

retain.title: How HashMap::retain works
retain.description: Keeps only the entries for which the closure returns true.

slides.caption: retain looks at every key and value and removes the entries that fail the test.
ann has 1: removed.
bo has 3: kept.
cy has 2: kept.
The closure gets the key too, so you can filter by either.

hashset-insert.title: How HashSet::insert works
hashset-insert.description: Adds a value; returns false if it was already there.

slides.caption: A HashSet holds every value at most once.
2 is new: added, and insert returns true.
2 is already there: nothing changes, insert returns false.
The returned bool is a cheap way to detect duplicates: if !seen.insert(x) { /* seen before */ }.

contains.title: How HashSet::contains works
contains.description: Checks whether a value is in the set, quickly.

slides.caption: contains hashes the value and checks one place, no matter how big the set is.
3 hashes to the slot that holds 3: true.
The other values are never compared.
For many lookups, collecting into a HashSet first is much faster than slice::contains.

union.title: How HashSet::union works
union.description: Every value that is in either set.

slides.caption: union yields the values of a, then the values of b that are not in a.
1 and 2 from a.
2 is in a already, so it is not repeated; 3 is new.
The result is an iterator of references; collect it into a HashSet to keep it. Its order is not fixed.

intersection.title: How HashSet::intersection works
intersection.description: Only the values that are in both sets.

slides.caption: intersection keeps a value only if both sets have it.
1 is only in a: left out.
2 and 3 are in both: kept.
4 is only in b: left out.
Useful for "what do these two lists have in common?".

difference.title: How HashSet::difference works
difference.description: The values in the first set that are not in the second.

slides.caption: difference starts from a and removes everything that b also has.
1 is not in b: kept.
2 and 3 are in b: removed.
4 is only in b, and b's own values never appear in the result.
Order matters: b.difference(&a) is {4}. symmetric_difference gives values in exactly one of them: {1, 4}.

is_subset.title: How HashSet::is_subset works
is_subset.description: true if every value of this set is also in the other.

slides.caption: is_subset checks each value of a against b.
1 is in b ✓
2 is in b ✓. Nothing in a is missing from b: true.
An empty set is a subset of every set. is_superset asks the opposite question.

symmetric_difference.title: How HashSet::symmetric_difference works
symmetric_difference.description: The values that are in exactly one of the two sets.

slides.caption: symmetric_difference drops the values both sets share.
2 and 3 are in both: dropped.
1 is only in a, 4 only in b: both kept.
Handy for "what changed between these two snapshots?".

from.title: How HashMap::from works
from.description: Builds a map from an array of (key, value) pairs.

slides.caption: from inserts the pairs in order, like calling insert for each.
("a", 1) and ("b", 2) are inserted.
("a", 3) replaces the earlier value of "a".
collect() from an iterator of pairs works the same way.
len counts the keys stored in the map.
Two keys: "a" and "b".
len() returns 2 instantly.
is_empty() is the same as len() == 0.

values.title: How HashMap::values works
values.description: An iterator over all the values, in no particular order.

note.text: order does not matter for a sum

slides.caption: values() yields every value once, in the map's internal (random) order.
1, 2 and 3 are visited in some order.
Their sum is 6, whatever the order.
Never rely on the order of a HashMap. Collect into a Vec and sort, or use a BTreeMap.

keys.title: How HashMap::keys works
keys.description: An iterator over all keys, in no particular order.

title.text: let mut k: Vec<_> = m.keys().collect(); k.sort();

slides.caption: keys() yields each key once, in random order, so sort if you print them.
The keys come out in some order.
Sorting gives a predictable ["a", "b"].
into_keys() consumes the map and gives owned keys.

iter.title: How HashMap::iter works
iter.description: An iterator over (key, value) pairs, in no particular order.

slides.caption: Iterating over &m gives (&key, &value) pairs.
Each entry is visited once.
The order can differ between runs: never depend on it.
Sorted output: let mut v: Vec<_> = m.iter().collect(); v.sort();

get_key_value.title: How HashMap::get_key_value works
get_key_value.description: Returns the stored key and its value.

slides.caption: Like get, but also gives back the key as it is stored in the map.
"a" is found.
Both the key and the value are returned.
Useful when equal-looking keys can differ in details you want to see.

or_insert_with_key.title: How Entry::or_insert_with_key works
or_insert_with_key.description: Like or_insert_with, but the closure gets the key.

slides.caption: When the default value depends on the key, the closure receives it.
"apple" is new: its value is its length, 5.
"kiwi": 4.
Saves cloning the key just to compute the default.

hashset-remove.title: How HashSet::remove works
hashset-remove.description: Removes a value; returns whether it was there.

slides.caption: remove takes the value out if present.
2 was there: removed, true.
9 was not: nothing happens, false.
take(&x) returns the removed value instead of a bool.

is_disjoint.title: How HashSet::is_disjoint works
is_disjoint.description: true if the two sets have nothing in common.

slides.caption: is_disjoint checks every value of one set against the other.
1 and 2 are not in b.
No value is shared: true.
The same as a.intersection(&b).next().is_none(), but clearer.

hashset-retain.title: How HashSet::retain works
hashset-retain.description: Keeps only the values that pass the test.

slides.caption: retain removes every value for which the closure says false.
1 and 3 are removed.
2 and 4 stay.
The set is changed in place.

new.title: How HashMap::new works
new.description: An empty map from keys to values.

slides.caption: new() allocates nothing until the first insert.
The map starts empty.
After insert it holds one pair.
The key and value types are usually inferred from the first insert.

with_capacity.title: How HashMap::with_capacity works
with_capacity.description: An empty map with room for n entries.

slides.caption: Growing a hash map means rehashing every key; reserving room avoids that.
Room for 100 entries.
Still empty.
Same idea as Vec::with_capacity.

capacity.title: How HashMap::capacity works
capacity.description: How many entries fit before the map must grow.

slides.caption: The map keeps spare room so inserts stay fast.
3 entries are stored.
Capacity is at least that.
The exact number is an implementation detail.

reserve.title: How HashMap::reserve works
reserve.description: Makes room for at least n more entries.

slides.caption: One growth step now instead of several during the inserts.
Room for 50 is requested.
Capacity is now at least 50.
try_reserve reports failure instead of aborting.

shrink_to_fit.title: How HashMap::shrink_to_fit works
shrink_to_fit.description: Releases spare room after many removals.

slides.caption: Removing entries never shrinks a map by itself.
Most of the room is unused.
It is released.
Capacity stays at least len.

is_empty.title: How HashMap::is_empty works
is_empty.description: true if the map has no entries.

slides.caption: is_empty reads better than len() == 0.
Empty: true.
One entry: false.
All std collections have is_empty.

clear.title: How HashMap::clear works
clear.description: Removes every entry, keeping the allocated room.

slides.caption: clear drops all keys and values; capacity stays for reuse.
Both entries are removed.
The map is empty.
drain() also removes everything, but hands the entries to you.

drain.title: How HashMap::drain works
drain.description: Removes every entry and gives each one to you.

slides.caption: The map ends up empty but keeps its capacity.
Each (key, value) pair is moved out.
The map is left empty.
Pairs come out in arbitrary order.

iter_mut.title: How HashMap::iter_mut works
iter_mut.description: Visits every entry with a mutable reference to its value.

slides.caption: Keys stay read-only; values can be changed.
Each value is lent mutably.
All are multiplied by 10.
values_mut() if you do not need the keys.
Like iter_mut, without the keys.
Each value is lent.
Each gets + 1.
Keys can never be changed in place; remove and re-insert instead.

into_keys.title: How HashMap::into_keys works
into_keys.description: Consumes the map and yields its keys (owned).

slides.caption: The values are dropped; the keys are moved out.
The map is consumed.
Its keys come out (sorted here for display).
into_values does the same for the values.

into_values.title: How HashMap::into_values works
into_values.description: Consumes the map and yields its values (owned).

slides.caption: Keys are dropped; values are moved out.
Values 3 and 1 come out.
Their sum is 4.
values() only borrows them.

remove_entry.title: How HashMap::remove_entry works
remove_entry.description: Removes a key and returns both the stored key and the value.

slides.caption: remove returns only the value; remove_entry returns the key too.
The entry for "id" is found.
It is removed and returned as a pair.
Useful when the key is an expensive String you want to reuse.

extract_if.title: How HashMap::extract_if works
extract_if.description: Removes the entries that pass a test and gives them to you.

slides.caption: retain keeps the passing entries; extract_if takes them out.
"b": 20 passes the test and is moved out.
The rest stays.
The closure may also change the values it sees.

get_disjoint_mut.title: How HashMap::get_disjoint_mut works
get_disjoint_mut.description: Mutable references to several different keys at once.

slides.caption: Two get_mut calls at once would not compile; this checks that the keys differ.
Both values are lent mutably.
30 moves from ann to bob.
It panics if the same key is listed twice.

extend.title: How HashMap::extend works
extend.description: Inserts every pair from an iterator; existing keys are overwritten.

slides.caption: extend is insert in a loop.
"a" already exists: its value becomes 9.
"b" is new.
Merging two maps: a.extend(b).

from_iter.title: How HashMap::from_iter works
from_iter.description: Builds a map from (key, value) pairs; this is what collect() uses.

slides.caption: Each pair is inserted; later duplicates overwrite earlier ones.
Pairs ("apple", 5) and ("kiwi", 4) are made.
They form the map.
HashMap::from([(k, v), ...]) is shorter for fixed data.

key.title: How Entry::key works
key.description: The key this entry is about, whether it exists or not.

slides.caption: Every Entry knows its key, occupied or vacant.
The entry for "pear" is created.
key() returns "pear".
Useful when the key was computed and you need it again.

insert_entry.title: How Entry::insert_entry works
insert_entry.description: Sets the value (new or replacing) and returns the occupied entry.

slides.caption: Whatever was there before, the key now maps to 5.
Vacant: inserted.
Occupied: replaced.
The returned OccupiedEntry lets you keep working with that entry.

occupied-get.title: How OccupiedEntry::get works
occupied-get.description: Reads the value of an entry that exists.

slides.caption: After matching Entry::Occupied, the value is guaranteed to be there.
"x" exists: Occupied.
get() lends its value.
Matching on Entry handles both cases with a single lookup.

occupied-insert.title: How OccupiedEntry::insert works
occupied-insert.description: Replaces the value and returns the old one.

slides.caption: The key stays; only the value changes.
The old 3 comes back.
10 is stored.
Same as HashMap::insert on an existing key.

occupied-remove.title: How OccupiedEntry::remove works
occupied-remove.description: Removes the entry and returns its value.

slides.caption: Decide based on the value, then remove, with one lookup.
The value 1 is returned.
The key is gone.
remove_entry also returns the key.

occupied-get_mut.title: How OccupiedEntry::get_mut works
occupied-get_mut.description: A mutable reference to the value, for as long as the entry lives.

slides.caption: Changes go straight into the map.
The value is lent mutably.
It becomes 2.
into_mut gives a reference that outlives the entry.

into_mut.title: How OccupiedEntry::into_mut works
into_mut.description: Turns the entry into a &mut to its value that lives on.

slides.caption: The entry is consumed; the reference is tied to the map instead.
The entry becomes a &mut Vec.
2 is pushed.
or_insert also returns such a reference.

vacant-insert.title: How VacantEntry::insert works
vacant-insert.description: Fills a missing key and returns &mut to the new value.

slides.caption: Only reached when the key did not exist.
"new" is missing: Vacant.
insert(0) creates it.
or_insert is the shortcut for this pattern.

into_key.title: How VacantEntry::into_key works
into_key.description: Gives the key back without inserting anything.

slides.caption: m.entry(key) took ownership of the key; into_key returns it.
The key is handed back.
Nothing was inserted.
Avoids cloning an expensive key just to look it up.

hashset-new.title: How HashSet::new works
hashset-new.description: An empty set: a collection of unique values.

slides.caption: A set remembers whether a value is in it, nothing more.
Empty.
After insert(3): {3}.
Classic use: tracking what you have already seen.
Inserting a value that is already present changes nothing.
The second 2 is ignored.
Three distinct values.
Count distinct words: words.iter().collect::<HashSet<_>>().len().

hashset-is_empty.title: How HashSet::is_empty works
hashset-is_empty.description: true if the set has no values.

slides.caption: A quick emptiness check.
Empty: true.
One value: false.
Handy in loops that process a work set until it is empty.

hashset-iter.title: How HashSet::iter works
hashset-iter.description: Visits every value, in no particular order.

slides.caption: Use iter for anything that does not depend on order, like sums or counts.
Each value is visited once.
Their sum is 6.
Need sorted output? Collect into a Vec and sort, or use a BTreeSet.

is_superset.title: How HashSet::is_superset works
is_superset.description: true if this set contains every value of the other.

slides.caption: Every element of b must be in a.
1 and 3 are both in a.
So a is a superset: true.
is_subset asks the reverse question.

hashset-get.title: How HashSet::get works
hashset-get.description: A reference to the stored value equal to the one given.

slides.caption: contains says yes or no; get returns the element itself.
"Ann" is in the set.
You get a reference to it.
Useful for interning: reuse the stored String instead of a new one.

take.title: How HashSet::take works
take.description: Removes a value and returns it.

slides.caption: remove returns a bool; take returns the owned value.
"a" comes out.
"b" stays.
Returns None if the value was not there.

replace.title: How HashSet::replace works
replace.description: Inserts a value, replacing an equal one, and returns the old one.

slides.caption: insert keeps the old element; replace swaps it for the new one.
1 was there: the old one is returned.
2 is new: None.
Matters when equal values still differ in other fields.

hashset-drain.title: How HashSet::drain works
hashset-drain.description: Removes every value and gives each one to you.

slides.caption: The set keeps its capacity for reuse.
Each value is moved out.
The set is empty.
Values come out in arbitrary order.
clear keeps the allocated room.
All values are dropped.
The set is empty.
Reuse the same set across loop iterations to avoid reallocating.

hashset-extract_if.title: How HashSet::extract_if works
hashset-extract_if.description: Removes the values that pass a test and gives them to you.

slides.caption: Like retain, but the removed values are not lost.
2 and 4 pass: taken out.
1 and 3 stay.
The iterator must be consumed for the removal to happen.

hashset-extend.title: How HashSet::extend works
hashset-extend.description: Inserts every value from an iterator; duplicates are ignored.

slides.caption: Values already present change nothing.
1 is already there.
2 is added once.
Union in place: a.extend(&b) for Copy values.

hashset-from_iter.title: How HashSet::from_iter works
hashset-from_iter.description: Builds a set from an iterator; this is what collect() uses.

slides.caption: Every item is inserted; duplicates collapse.
"b", "a", "b" go in.
Two distinct values remain.
The quickest way to remove duplicates when order does not matter.
